name: A run in the middle
why: This is the main case. If both numbers are the same index, the search stopped at the first 7 it found. Each end needs its own search for a boundary, which keeps going after it finds a 7.

name: A single copy
why: With only one copy, the first and last index are the same. An answer like [2, 3] means the second search returned the first value bigger than t, without subtracting 1.

name: Not in the list
why: A boundary search always returns an index, even when t is not in the list. After it, check that the value at that index really is t.

name: The run starts the list
why: The first copy is at index 0, so the search must be able to end at 0. Check the branch that keeps mid when times[mid] >= t.

name: The run ends the list
why: No value is bigger than 9, so the first value bigger than t is one past the end, at index 4. With a half-open window, hi must start at len(times) so that this answer is possible.

name: Every value the same
why: Both boundaries are at the ends of the list. A search that stops at the first 7 it finds returns the middle index, 4.

name: Empty list
why: The boundary is index 0, which is not a valid position in an empty list. Check that the index is inside the list before you read times[i].

name: Half a million copies, at most 60 reads
show: times = ten 1s, then 500,000 copies of 5, then ten 9s; t = 5
why: This list counts reads. If you find one 5 and then step left and right, you read every copy: half a million reads. Two boundary searches need about 20 reads each.

name: Not in the list, between two long runs
show: times = 300,000 copies of 1, then 300,000 copies of 9; t = 5
why: The first value that is 5 or more is a 9, so 5 is not in the list. Going through the list one by one reads 300,000 values to find this out. A boundary search reads about 20.
